title: How Landslides Happen
objective: After this level you can explain how slope, water and gravity combine to send rock and soil sliding downhill.
summary: A landslide is gravity beating a slope's strength. Water cuts friction and adds weight; undercutting, quakes and digging trigger slides, and burned slopes can unleash fast debris flows.

cards.headline: Debris flows often move faster than a person can run.
cards.body: A hillside can hold still for years, then let go in minutes. Gravity pulls on every slope, all the time. The real question is what finally lets it win.

cards.headline: A tug-of-war on every hill
cards.body: A landslide is a mass of rock, debris or earth moving down a slope. Every slope is a tug-of-war: gravity pulls material downhill, while the material's own strength holds it in place. When the pull wins, the slope fails. Geologists sort the result by how it moves: falls, topples, slides, spreads and flows.

cards.headline: What tips the balance
cards.body: Rain and snowmelt are classic triggers. Soak a sandy slope and the water cuts the friction between its grains; a rising water table adds load, too. A stream cutting into the foot of a slope oversteepens it, and so does digging for roads or buildings. Earthquakes can shake a slope loose. Landslides happen in every US state and territory.

cards.headline: When fire comes first
cards.body: Debris flows are among the fastest and most dangerous kinds: water, mud, rocks and plants surging downhill like flowing concrete, at speeds that can top 35 mph. They are a special hazard after wildfire. With the plants gone and the soil changed, burned ground soaks up less rain, so even a modest storm can set off a debris flow on a steep slope.

questions.prompt: Why are steep slopes especially prone to debris flows after a wildfire?

options.label: Ash makes the soil heavier than rock
options.rationale: Weight of ash isn't the reason given.

options.label: Fire melts the rock into mud
options.rationale: Fire doesn't melt rock on a hillside.

options.label: Wind blows the loose soil downhill
options.rationale: Debris flows are driven by water and gravity.

options.label: Burned ground absorbs less rain, so storms run off

questions.explanation: With plants gone and soil changed, burned ground soaks up less rain, so even modest storms can trigger debris flows.

questions.prompt: How does soaking rain help trigger a landslide on a sandy slope?

options.label: It freezes and glues the grains together
options.rationale: That would make the slope stronger, not weaker.

options.label: It cuts friction between grains and adds weight
It dissolves all the sand away
options.rationale: Sand grains are mostly quartz, which barely dissolves.

options.label: It makes the slope less steep
options.rationale: Water doesn't flatten the slope before it fails.

questions.explanation: Water reduces the friction between sand grains, and a rising water table loads the slope, tipping the balance toward failure.

questions.prompt: Match each landslide trigger with how it works.

pairs.right: Burned ground soaks up less rain

questions.explanation: A stream cutting into the foot of a slope oversteepens it, earthquakes shake a slope loose, and after wildfire, burned ground soaks up less rain.
